turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Doctor: Hello, I’m your doctor today. What brings you in today? Patient: I’m here for my annual check-up, and I’ve noticed a rough, scaly, sandpaper-like patch on the back of my left hand that doesn’t hurt or feel tender.
Doctor: How long have you had this rough, scaly patch on the back of your left hand?
Patient: I’ve had it for a few months now, and it seems to be staying about the same without any pain or tenderness.
Doctor: Do you notice any itching, burning, or other sensations associated with the patch?
Patient: No, it doesn’t itch or burn—there aren’t really any sensations there, and it hasn’t caused pain or tenderness.
Doctor: Have you had a lot of sun exposure or outdoor work that involves your hands, especially on the back of the left hand?
Patient: Yes, I do a fair amount of outdoor walking and I’ve often spent time sunbathing, so my hands—especially the backs—get a lot of sun exposure.
Doctor: How large is the patch, and what does it look like in terms of color and border—does it have well‑defined edges or look more irregular?

Patient: It’s about the size of a small coin, kind of light brown to reddish, with a rough, scaly surface. The edges feel fairly well-defined, though the border isn’t perfectly straight and can look a bit irregular.
Doctor: Have you noticed any bleeding, crusting, or ulceration of the patch, or does it ever weep or ooze?
Patient: No, it hasn’t bled or crusted over, and I haven’t noticed any ulcer or weeping or oozing from the patch. It just stays as a rough, scaly area without pain or tenderness.
Doctor: Have you noticed any other rough or scaly spots on sun‑exposed areas of your body, such as your face, forearms, or scalp?
Patient: I haven’t really noticed any other similar rough, scaly spots on my face, forearms, or scalp—this one on the back of my left hand is the only spot like that.
Doctor: May I ask how old you are and what your typical skin type is (for example, do you tend to burn easily, tan, or have a lot of freckles)?
Patient: I’m 65 years old, and I tend to tan more than burn when I’m out in the sun; I don’t have a lot of freckles.
Doctor:

Patient: I don’t have any other similar rough patches, and this one has stayed about the same for a few months. It’s light brown to reddish, coin-sized, with a rough scaly texture, and it hasn’t bled, crusted, or caused pain. Given my sun exposure on my walks and sunbathing, I’m mostly concerned about what this patch could be.
Doctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with skin cancer or had any previous biopsies of skin lesions?
Patient: No, I haven’t ever been diagnosed with skin cancer, and I’ve never had a skin biopsy or any similar procedure done.
Doctor: Is the patch raised or flat when you run your fingers over it?
Patient: It feels raised a bit, and when I run my fingers over it, it still feels rough and scaly rather than smooth.
Doctor: Do you have a personal or family history of skin cancer or any previous skin lesions that were removed?
Patient: I don’t have any personal history of skin cancer, and I haven’t had any skin lesions removed before. As for my family, I’m not aware of any relatives who had skin cancer either.
